title: Nearly 9 in 10 Indian Adults Have Abnormal Cholesterol, Massive ICMR Study Finds
excerpt: A landmark nationwide study reveals 87.3% of Indian adults have at least one abnormal lipid level, with dyslipidemia peaking in the 30-39 age group — even among those with no other known risk factors.
body:
• The ICMR-INDIAB study of 23,665 adults found that 87.3% of Indian adults have at least one abnormal lipid level, making dyslipidemia one of the country's most widespread health problems.
  • An estimated 355 million Indians have abnormal cholesterol despite having normal blood sugar, blood pressure, and body weight — challenging standard screening practices.
  • Low HDL ("good" cholesterol) is the most common abnormality, affecting nearly two-thirds of Indian adults, with genetic predisposition compounded by carbohydrate-heavy diets.
  • Standard global heart risk calculators may be failing Indians — a separate GB Pant Hospital study found nearly 80% of first heart attack patients were never flagged as high-risk.

The Numbers Behind the Crisis

A nationally representative study by the Indian Council of Medical Research has delivered a stark finding: 87.3 per cent of Indian adults have an unhealthy balance of fats in their blood. The research, part of the ICMR-INDIAB study, analysed lipid profiles of 23,665 adults across all states and Union Territories.

Low high-density lipoprotein (HDL), commonly known as "good" cholesterol, was the most prevalent abnormality, affecting nearly two-thirds of all adults tested. Elevated LDL, high triglycerides, and high total cholesterol followed closely behind.

Perhaps the most alarming finding: an estimated 355 million Indians have abnormal lipid levels despite having normal blood sugar, normal blood pressure, and no obesity. That number alone challenges the widespread medical practice of testing cholesterol only in patients who already have diabetes or hypertension.

"Indians are genetically predisposed to low HDL cholesterol, but lifestyle factors play an equally important role."

— Dr V Mohan, Chairman, Dr Mohan's Diabetes Specialities Centre and study co-author

Why It Hits Earlier Than Expected

The ICMR data showed that dyslipidemia peaks between the ages of 30 and 39 — a decade earlier than many clinicians expect. Women had a higher prevalence than men, while urban residents were more affected than rural populations, though the gap was narrower than anticipated.

A separate analysis by Metropolis Healthcare, based on 3.9 lakh lipid profile tests, reinforced these findings. One in four individuals showed abnormal cholesterol levels, with 35% exhibiting low HDL. More than one in three young adults aged 19–30 already had low HDL, and nearly 17% showed borderline high cholesterol.

These abnormalities are increasingly independent of obesity. Many individuals who appear healthy by conventional measures still present with low HDL and elevated triglycerides, pointing to diet quality, sedentary behaviour, and stress as the primary drivers.

The South Asian Phenotype Problem

A study led by Dr Mohit Dayal Gupta at GB Pant Hospital, analysing data from over 5,000 patients, found that nearly 80% of individuals who suffered their first heart attack had not been flagged as high-risk by standard global risk calculators. Only 11% to 20% were classified as high-risk using Western-derived models — despite all eventually experiencing cardiac events.

The gap traces back to what researchers call the "South Asian phenotype" — a distinct cluster of metabolic traits that include higher rates of diabetes and insulin resistance at younger ages, lower HDL levels, higher triglycerides even when LDL appears normal, and increased abdominal fat in people with normal body weight.

Additionally, markers like lipoprotein(a), ApoB levels, and central obesity are often not adequately captured in global risk tools, creating what cardiologists call a dangerous grey zone where real risks go undetected.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For Indians abroad, the findings carry particular weight. The South Asian phenotype travels with the population — genetic predisposition to lower HDL and higher triglycerides does not change with geography. Indians in the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada face the same elevated cardiovascular risk, often compounded by dietary shifts that increase processed food consumption while maintaining carbohydrate-heavy meal patterns.

Standard cholesterol panels in Western healthcare systems may not capture the full picture for South Asian patients. Experts recommend requesting comprehensive lipid panels that include lipoprotein(a) and ApoB levels, particularly for those with a family history of early heart disease.

Diet, Screening, and What Needs to Change

Dr V Mohan recommended the "plate concept" — one-quarter carbohydrates, one-quarter protein, and half the plate consisting of vegetables and fruits — as a practical dietary intervention. The ICMR study also called for broader cholesterol screening that extends beyond patients with pre-existing conditions, earlier detection in younger age groups, and lifestyle interventions including regular exercise, healthier diets, and reduced consumption of ultra-processed foods and trans fats.

The broader message from cardiologists is clear: "normal" test results do not always mean low risk for Indian patients. A more personalised, India-specific approach to cardiovascular risk assessment — one that accounts for genetic predisposition, dietary patterns, and metabolic markers unique to South Asian populations — could be key to preventing the next wave of premature heart disease.
nri_angle: South Asian genetic predisposition to low HDL and abnormal lipid levels persists regardless of geography, making comprehensive lipid panels critical for diaspora Indians in Western healthcare systems.
